overview: The DHT11 and DHT22 are the default 'read the room's temperature and humidity' sensors, both using a single data wire and a proprietary timing-based digital protocol instead of I2C or SPI — the microcontroller sends a short start signal, then reads back a precisely-timed sequence of pulses encoding 40 bits of data. The DHT22 costs more but is meaningfully better in every measurable way (wider range, better accuracy, faster response); the DHT11 remains popular purely because it's cheaper and 'good enough' for room-temperature hobby projects. Both are quite slow — readings should be requested no more than about once every 1-2 seconds, or the sensor returns stale/invalid data.
simpleSummary: A simple sensor that reports the room's temperature and humidity over a single wire.

specifications.samplingRate: DHT11: ~1 Hz max; DHT22: ~0.5 Hz max

pinMap.name: DATA
pinMap.function: Single-wire data line carrying both the request signal (from the microcontroller) and the 40-bit response (from the sensor), using precise pulse-width timing rather than a standard protocol.
pinMap.voltageRange: 0-5V, needs a ~10kΩ pull-up resistor to VCC
pinMap.gotcha: Requesting data faster than the sensor's minimum interval (~1-2 seconds) returns garbage or a timeout — this is the most common 'my readings are all NaN' beginner problem.

useCases.title: Home weather station
useCases.scenario: Log or display indoor temperature and humidity over time.

useCases.title: Greenhouse/incubator climate control
useCases.scenario: Trigger a fan, heater, or humidifier based on threshold readings.

useCases.title: HVAC/smart thermostat prototype
useCases.scenario: Read ambient conditions as input to a simple climate control algorithm.

oftenConfusedWith: BME280 (I2C interface, adds pressure, better accuracy, costs more)
oftenUpgradedTo: BME280 for higher accuracy and a standard I2C interface instead of proprietary timing
